subject: physics
title: Circular Motion and Centripetal Force
welcome_lead: Round the bend with centripetal acceleration v²/r — and meet angular velocity along the way.
meta_desc: A-Level Further Mechanics adventure on circular motion and centripetal force.
final_note: Centripetal force always points to the centre — it changes direction, not speed.

concepts.def: v = ω r along the circular path.
F = m v² / r = m ω² r.
Time for one full revolution: T = 2π / ω.
Tilting a track so component of N provides force.

walkthroughs.body_html: ω is angle swept per second in radians. Full revolution = 2π rad, so ω = 2π / T = 2π f. Linear v = ω r.
Even at constant speed, direction changes, so there is acceleration a = v²/r = ω² r. This points to the centre of the circle.
F_c = m v²/r. The actual source varies: tension on a string, friction on a road, gravity in orbit, normal force on a banked curve.

options: Tangential
Towards the centre
Outward
Vertical

mcqs.q: Centripetal force on mass m at speed v in circle r is:
options: m v / r
m v² / r
m r / v²
m r v

mcqs.q: What force keeps a car moving in a circle around a bend?
options: A centrifugal force pushes the car outwards from the centre.
Friction from the road acting towards the centre of the circle — centripetal force.
Only if it speeds up or slows down on the circle.
The car's own momentum acts as a force that drives it in a circle.

mcqs.q: An object moves in a circle at constant speed. Is it accelerating?
options: Only if it speeds up or slows down on the circle.
Yes — its direction is constantly changing, so its velocity changes; centripetal acceleration points toward the centre of the circle.
The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.
No — constant speed means no acceleration.

mcqs.q: If an object is moving at constant velocity in a straight line, what is the net force on it?
options: There must be a forward force on the object to keep it moving.
Only if it speeds up or slows down on the circle.
The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.
Zero — by Newton's first law, constant velocity requires zero net force.
